points.description: Translates the triangulation into a tree (e.g. triangles as vertices, diagonals as edges, with 18n vertices and max degree 3), so each diagonal splits the triangles into two sides and the counts of triangles on each side can be tracked.

levels.says: Mentions the dual graph or tree but does not use its structure (such as degree at most 3) correctly.

points.description: Finds a first diagonal with at least 3n triangles on one side, and chooses it (e.g. by moving along the tree toward the larger side) so that the side is as small as possible or the split is balanced. Shows the part sizes are controlled, e.g. one side has at least 3n triangles and the other side is at most 9n. Equivalent balancing or modification argument is accepted.

levels.says: Finds a diagonal with at least 3n triangles on one side but does not control the other side's size, or the argument is incomplete.

points.description: Applies the argument again on the larger remaining side with the same hypotheses to find a second diagonal. This cuts that side into two parts, and the second diagonal is chosen so the new parts are also in the range.

levels.says: Attempts a second cut on one side but the hypotheses of the original cut are not satisfied, or there are errors.

points.description: Verifies that all three resulting parts contain at least 3n and at most 9n triangles. The verification uses the total of 18n triangles, and the two diagonals are counted correctly so the three counts sum to 18n.

levels.says: Checks only some of the bounds, or does not check the lower or upper bound for every part.

rubric.notes: Full marks need a complete, correct proof: tree model, a first balanced diagonal, a second diagonal found with the same hypotheses, and all three parts shown to be between 3n and 9n. Part marks go for the tree model, a first diagonal with at least 3n triangles, or an attempted second cut with errors. Equivalent wording and correct alternative methods earn full marks.
